title: The Revolution in Services: General Catalyst's AI Rollup Strategy, with Marc Bhargava
author: Marc Bhargava · Nathan Labenz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Bhargava supports selective automation embedded in human-designed workflows and expects a durable hybrid workforce in regulated, complex professional services. Labenz, however, argues that improving foundation models may erode contextual barriers, make AI outperform human–AI teams on some tasks and shift bounded services from augmentation toward substitution. The discussion therefore provides substantive support for the cluster’s near-term model while disputing its durability.
qs: But in services, think there's still gonna be a huge portion of lawyers, accountants, to your example, doctors, and instead there'll just be different steps that are automated but there'll be key people and it'll be this hybrid AI enabled workforce.

There's been some that have shown that like the hybrid, you know, there's always this like refuge that people want to take and well, it'll be the doctor and the AI that'll work together, but there's been some suggestive evidence at least that like, the AI is actually performing the best, then comes the hybrid, and then the doctor alone is worse.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core hybrid-service proposition: AI automates a substantial share of professional tasks while lawyers remain necessary. It materially extends the synthesis with an investment thesis that quantifies potential margin expansion and increased service capacity from partial workflow automation, including reduced outsourcing by in-house legal teams. These are forecasts rather than independently established outcomes.
qs: So we don't think that lawyers or accountants or IT specialists or HOA managers or any of those jobs are going away, but we think 30 to 70% of the tasks they do can be automated, and this frees them up to do more elsewhere.
So instead of something like 5 to 10% EBITDA margins, 30 to 40% in certain cases, if you flow through the level of automation at, you know, 50% plus.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Bhargava supports the cluster’s core proposition that multistep services work will combine delegated AI execution with human intervention rather than default to fully autonomous agents. He specifically favors structured hybrid workflows in which individual steps may be automated while the overall process remains divided between humans and AI. The excerpt is predictive and conceptual, not evidence of deployment reliability or reduced verification needs.
qs: **Marc Bhargava:** [(51:59)](https://youtube.com/watch?v=gT-qbKTHv6Y&t=3119s&ref=cognitiverevolution.ai) So on the services side, I think it's gonna be more of the first case that you outlined where there are 7 or 8 steps and some of them will be automated and maybe a AI agent or does step 1, a human does step 2.
And so it's gonna be these hybrid AI enabled workforces where there are multiple steps and some are fully automated, some are not.

kp.k: AI rollups combine software, services, and acquisitions
kp.d: Marc Bhargava describes an investment model in which applied-AI companies acquire established service providers to obtain distribution, client relationships, proprietary data, and feedback loops. Acquired businesses are then intended to generate more free cash flow through automation, supporting further acquisitions and organic growth.
qs: In many cases, these are in the services businesses where we actually will need to go and buy our distribution base or buy our client list in order to get these to market, in order to get the proprietary data to continue to train and improve the models.

We think there's a new generation of compounders. We wanna create those. We wanna incubate those. And we think a big part of that story will be the AI automation around how they're improving those businesses.

kp.k: Services offer a much larger addressable market
kp.d: Bhargava frames AI-enabled services as a venture opportunity because global services revenue is asserted to be $16 trillion annually, compared with $1 trillion for software. He argues that automating 30–70% of workflows could transform services businesses from 5–10% EBITDA margins to 30–40% margins in some cases; these are investment-thesis projections rather than independently established findings in the transcript.
qs: So globally, services is a 16,000,000,000,000 a year revenue opportunity. Software is actually only a 1,000,000,000,000 global revenue opportunity.
Now if you're automating 30 to 70% of the workflows in some of these services industries, you can AI enable the workforce and take a lot more clients.
So instead of something like 5 to 10% EBITDA margins, 30 to 40% in certain cases, if you flow through the level of automation at, you know, 50% plus.

kp.k: Legal delivery shifts toward selling completed work
kp.d: Bhargava argues that AI blurs the boundary between software and labour, making hybrid providers that sell outcomes or completed work increasingly attractive. In legal services, where he says most spending goes to third-party law firms rather than software, the proposed model combines AI software with service delivery instead of merely selling tools to incumbent firms.
qs: Yeah. It really now is about selling work.
Most legal spend is really on third party law firms. It's not really on the software component compared to the spend on lawyers.
And so I think, and it's been reported of course, that this hybrid services plus software is getting more and more interesting because the margin profile is changing in services.

kp.k: AI may move legal work in-house
kp.d: Bhargava presents UDIA as an example of a provider selling Fortune 100 in-house legal teams a combination of AI-enabled software and services. The claimed customer proposition is to reduce reliance on third-party law firms by enabling in-house counsel to perform more work, including NDAs and contracts, without proportionate staff growth.
qs: Most legal spend is really on third party law firms.

And so, you know, an approach that 1 of our portfolio companies, UDIA, is taking is they are going after Fortune 100 general counsels in house law firms, and they're selling to them a mix of services and software, all AI enabled so that, you know, these Fortune 100 brands can spend less on third party lawyers and instead do more in house with the tool set UD is giving them, which is a mix of software to do things like NDAs and contracts, but also services.

Udia being a great example of coming in and helping these large corporations have their in house legal teams be AI enabled and take on more work with, you know, the same number of people and outsource less to these third party law firms.

kp.k: Legal automation targets tasks, not whole professions
kp.d: Bhargava says General Catalyst underwrites complementary, human-in-the-loop systems rather than full replacement of lawyers or other professionals. Its premise is that 30–70% of tasks may be automated while lawyers remain responsible for complex transactions, regulated work, judgement, and interpersonal activity; he expressly excludes fully automatable fields from this rollup strategy.
qs: Question, we're really underwriting complimentary AI services.

So we don't think that lawyers or accountants or IT specialists or HOA managers or any of those jobs are going away, but we think 30 to 70% of the tasks they do can be automated, and this frees them up to do more elsewhere.
We're not really doing the strategy if we think something can be a 100% automated.

But for legal or for accounting, we absolutely think on large deals, large transactions, preparing your taxes, even on or with call centers, you know, there are more emotional calls, more difficult ones. In all of these cases, it's about AI enablement of the human team and being able to do more.

kp.k: Hybrid workflows retain lawyers at critical steps
kp.d: For professional services, Bhargava expects structured workflows in which some steps are automated and others remain human. He grounds this expectation in current technical limitations, regulation, emotional and relational dimensions, complexity, and the need for judgement in grey areas, rather than claiming that autonomous agents can presently replace lawyers end to end.
qs: So on the services side, I think it's gonna be more of the first case that you outlined where there are 7 or 8 steps and some of them will be automated and maybe a AI agent or does step 1, a human does step 2.
And so it's gonna be these hybrid AI enabled workforces where there are multiple steps and some are fully automated, some are not.

But in services, think there's still gonna be a huge portion of lawyers, accountants, to your example, doctors, and instead there'll just be different steps that are automated but there'll be key people and it'll be this hybrid AI enabled workforce.

But in the industries I'm focused on in applied AI, especially a lot of the services industries which we discussed is really large part of the global economy, I think it will be a hybrid approach because of the human element, because of the regulatory element, because of the complexity and sort of gray areas of tasks.

kp.k: Reasoning models expand automatable legal work
kp.d: Bhargava identifies logic and reasoning as a newer automation category enabled by improving models. His legal example is AI helping lawyers anticipate questions they may face in a case, positioning the model as a preparatory aid that supplies a provisional answer while a human remains in the loop.
qs: And now fourth, more recently is around logic and reasoning.
And as models are getting better at logic and reasoning and math, you can have more AI tools kind of with a human in the loop giving you kind of a quasi answer to what you might want to do or say.
Legal is also a good example of this where now Anthropic and others have created models that are quite good at reasoning.
And so a lawyer can say, well, you know, what cases am I gonna what questions am I gonna get on my case? And so you can start to do this like more human prep.

kp.k: AI could make legal departments more proactive
kp.d: Bhargava predicts that legal work may evolve beyond reactive cost-centre functions. He gives the example of comparing contracts to identify inconsistencies and recommend pricing changes, potentially allowing law firms or legal departments to contribute business recommendations as well as complete conventional legal tasks.
qs: But even how you visualize the product certainly will change over time with AI as it we're seeing in things like legal being a great example of this where lawyers can also compare all the contracts and then recommend pricing changes because there's inconsistencies.
So how does the law firm or the legal department go from just a cost center to also making recommendations and maybe being even a business plus center, and AI can make that change.

And the second is to change the output of these services businesses and things like accounting or legal start to be more diagnostic, more prescriptive, more insightful, and become departments that aren't just thought of as a cost center or a check the box, but can actually help you in running your business.

kp.k: Model selection varies by legal task
kp.d: Bhargava reports an internal observation from UDIA that different foundation models perform better for different legal functions: OpenAI for summarising case text and Anthropic for reasoning and generating difficult courtroom questions. He argues that legal providers therefore need technical expertise to evaluate, combine, and update multiple models as they improve.
qs: For example, with legal, at least, found that, you know, OpenAI is really great at summarization of case text, for example, but the Anthropic model is better at reasoning and asking difficult questions that you might face in a courtroom.

And so having kind of both OpenAI and Anthropic every 3 to 6 months improving their models, you know, we flow both of those through at UDIA to deliver value for the end client, is the in house general counsel at a Fortune 100 firm.

And so you have to have this technology and AI expertise to understand the different models, where to use which 1, and where there are also point solutions that are already built, you know, you have to have the technical expertise to evaluate them and integrate them as well.

kp.k: Vertical platforms integrate fragmented legal point solutions
kp.d: Bhargava says legal and other service markets already contain many technology products, but characterises them as point solutions lacking full-platform integration, customisation, or training on provider-specific data. He argues that AI-native service companies need strong technical leadership to stitch products together, build custom components, choose models, and use proprietary datasets.
qs: There's a lot of middle ground because there are many point solutions out there in a lot of these industries, legal, accounting, IT, customer support call centers.
Generally, they're point solutions. Generally, it's not a full platform play. Generally, they're not customized, and generally, they're not trained on your proprietary data.

So there's still a lot left and that's why at the core of these transformations is staffing a great backing great founders who are great technologists because there's a lot to do in terms of stitching together different point solutions.
There's a lot to do in terms of creating custom solutions. There's a lot to do on fine training models and making it unique to your dataset.

kp.k: Acquisitions provide data and faster feedback
kp.d: The rollup's claimed competitive advantage is not separate technology for every acquired firm, but a substantially standard solution deployed across firms in the same vertical. Acquisitions provide proprietary operational data and faster customer feedback, which Bhargava says can improve software and model training relative to vendors lacking equivalent access.
qs: If you buy 10 IT firms, 10 call centers, 10 accounting firms, 10 legal service firms, 10 HOA management firms, The solution base that we're building for each is the same.
So there's some slight customization, but it's extremely similar.

But what we do see as unique is as we buy these companies, we do get their proprietary data, we can feed it in, and we can train models, and we can adjust our software based on having proprietary data and much faster feedback loops on what the client wants.

So ultimately, we think our product is, you know, much better on market than someone who maybe isn't doing a rollup strategy that does not have access to their client's data, that does not have as fast a feedback loop.

kp.k: Workflow mapping precedes acquisition and automation
kp.d: The operational method is to shadow staff, map workflows and hours, and identify tasks fitting four automation categories: customer support, content creation, repetitive data work, and increasingly logic and reasoning. Initial sector screening is followed by granular pilot-customer evidence; further capital is conditional on demonstrating useful software, customer traction, and the claimed automation level before acquiring a target.
qs: Yeah. Generally, we think about it by going in there and shadowing the customer and understanding all the workflows in their business.
And so then we add up who are all the folks, what are their workflows, and we map out the hours at a company.
Then what we do is we go through those workflows and hours worked and we look at where could AI automate some of these workflows.
And then once we've actually given the first round of funding, in order to get the second round of funding from us, then the team needs to go out and really get the data.

So we do a first round of analysis in mapping it and looking at the industries. As we start placing bets, then of course, the team has an even higher bar to build an AI native software product that is very useful and to go and win an initial set of clients and then to come back to us and prove to us the automation with those clients.

kp.k: Pilot customers can become acquisition targets
kp.d: The proposed sequence is to build software, secure roughly 10–15 clients in the cited call-centre example, prove substantial automation, and then acquire a larger service business—often an existing client. Owners may accept cash plus rollover equity because they have observed the technology and expect upside from the broader compounder, while retained leadership supplies alignment and implementation capacity.
qs: You know, Crexendo, the call center rollup is a good example where they got to 10, 15 different clients. They had a smaller sort of revenue base, they were selling in and had a high degree of automation.
And that's when we said, okay, we should actually buy a call center that does, you know, more meaningful amount of revenue.

So you actually see a lot of the pilot clients or customers say, hey, this is the writing on the wall. We're seeing this automation, but we might not necessarily be able to fully implement it. We would like to sell to you.
So the more classic version of it is, you know, we go out, we get customers, we get pilots, we start working with folks.

We also get a sense of which of these companies want the technology transformation, which of them get it. And we put a premium on that and we try to buy those style companies cause our goal is really revenue increasing.

kp.k: Adoption depends on leadership pull and familiar workflows
kp.d: Bhargava recommends selecting acquisition targets whose leaders already want technological transformation, even if that requires paying a premium. After acquisition, systems should preserve familiar email, text, or other existing workflows rather than impose entirely new interfaces, reducing training and adoption burdens while AI operates behind the scenes.
qs: I think a big learning for us is to find the assets and the companies that have a pull factor.

Does this client really want the technology transformation? Have they tried different products? Have they tried hiring people? Have they really pushed through at the leadership level that they want technology and AI?
And we will pay a premium or our companies pay a premium in the acquisition to have the right partner and the right partner mindset.
So we're not trying to onboard you to some new software tool.

We're generally mapping over those same workflows and so it's not a big change many times for the workforce to actually learn and adopt these toolings because our companies are building the tooling to be very similar to what they do day to day.

kp.k: Growth strategy contrasts with private-equity cost cutting
kp.d: Bhargava contrasts AI rollups with private-equity consolidation. Rather than eliminate overlapping staff and use savings to service acquisition debt, his stated strategy retains management, adds spending on engineers and software, and seeks margin expansion by allowing the same workforce to serve more clients. He acknowledges that the thesis succeeds only if genuine productivity gains materialise.
qs: Because it's saying if we buy 2 firms that do the exact thing, there's obviously overlap. Could we remove some of the overlap people? This saves cost. With this cost saving, we could pay interest payments on our debt and so we could finance these with debt and that's the model.

We are trying to come in with an alternative option which is same management, same team, let's AI enable it, let's go for more revenue rather than less cost cutting and that's our path to higher margin.

And we're only right if the AI enablement works because if we're asking you to go and take twice as many clients with the same group of people, that's just not gonna match up unless we're really giving you the tools so that each person can do twice as much work.
So we really need to get this AI automation right in order for our thesis to play out.

kp.k: Investment target is doubled revenue, not layoffs
kp.d: Bhargava supplies a three-year underwriting target: increase costs by 20% for software, engineers, and AI tools while doubling revenue. He repeatedly characterises the approach as automating tasks rather than people and argues that greater worker productivity should support hiring and economic growth; these are strategic objectives and predictions, not demonstrated labour-market outcomes.
qs: We're automating people. We're automating tasks. So automating maybe 30% or 30 50% of the tasks that they're doing which enables them to do harder tasks which generally are higher margin and to cross sell as well.
If you go in and you AI AI enable a workforce, you can now take on twice as much work with the same team because they have more tools and they're automating away the easier tasks.
I think, ideally, in a 3 year period, we would like folks to be with the 20% cost increase, be able to double your revenue.

But in 3 years, if we come in, we spend 20% more than you spend today to make sure you have the right software, the right engineers, the right AI tools, increase the cost 20%, can we increase the revenue a 100% in a 3 year period?

kp.k: Worker transition is framed as augmentation
kp.d: Bhargava reports initial employee apprehension but says acquired firms are told that AI will enable rather than replace their workforces. The intended change is removal of repetitive work and reassignment toward harder, higher-value, and human-facing tasks; later acquisitions can be reassured through prior implementation case studies. The transcript does not provide workforce counts or independent evidence of retention outcomes.
qs: I think there is, you know, at first a bit of apprehension around any new tool or technology.
So we are not coming in here to replace the workforce but to AI enable it and to take on more customers and have more revenue and have a growth story.
Generally though, we're saving them from the most mundane or boring parts of their day or the most repetitive parts of their day.
So we are freeing them up to do generally more interesting, more demanding and more human to human kind of interactive tasks.
We give you the software and tools to automate your mundane tasks, you get to do harder workflows, you know, it ends up being better for the company, your shares are worth more.

kp.k: Labenz predicts greater employment disruption
kp.d: Host Nathan Labenz—not Bhargava—argues that very high task automation may ultimately displace workers because demand for services such as accounting may not expand tenfold. He speculates that human-centred sectors including nursing, childcare, eldercare, and education may be better able to absorb displaced workers, while still expecting substantial consumer benefits.
qs: But when we're talking about 90% plus task automation, potentially in just the next 1 to 2 years, do we really need 10 times more accounting, for example, even at lower prices?
I'm sure there's some latent demand to be unlocked, but my intuition is that many workers in fields like accounting will ultimately be displaced.

And if I had to guess, I would bet on human centric fields like nursing, childcare, eldercare, and education as the sectors with sufficiently elastic demand so as to potentially absorb those AI refugees.

Bottom line, I believe that the land of abundance that Marc envisions is likely to materialize, and I look forward to it while at the same time expecting that the transition could well be far more disruptive than he projects.

kp.k: Bhargava predicts agent-managed professional workforces
kp.d: In response to displacement concerns, Bhargava predicts that individuals will manage teams of AI agents and that economic expansion will create additional work. He concedes that particular jobs may disappear and that the distribution of lost and newly created roles is difficult to forecast, while maintaining that the current portfolio strategy focuses on reallocating tasks rather than replacing jobs.
qs: Yeah. I think for us, you know, it'll be a lot of individuals will manage teams of agents.
Not necessarily. Like I do think that the overall economic growth and GDP output can grow pretty significantly.

And so we'll kind of have this land of abundance where people are still doing jobs but with teams of agents below them, but there are way more jobs to be do done because it's such a larger global economy.
It is very hard to predict and lay out exactly, like, what's the overall economic growth? You know, what does that mean in terms of new jobs? Which jobs are lost? Which jobs are gained?

But at least as far as we're seeing in the cases of hybrid services, software, AI enabled, you know, the strategy we're doing is not around really replacing jobs. It's freeing people up to do other tasks.

kp.k: Legal rollups require multidisciplinary founding teams
kp.d: Bhargava argues that successful AI-enabled rollups need both applied-AI expertise and service-industry, M&A, and private-equity operating experience. General Catalyst's role is to identify promising sectors and assemble teams capable of building legal or other vertical software while also acquiring and integrating service providers.
qs: And so in many of these cases, what we've done is we've found people who have led applied AI teams at places like RipLang or RAM or Scale AI. We're kind of combining them with industry experts who have done m and a before, done rollups before.
We're putting together both of those legs.

And so that's a really important part of where GC fits into this is identifying which industries have high potential for automation, but then also putting together a founding team that can do the automation, has experience in applied AI, and has experience in the industry, in m and a, in private equity, and doing the buyout part as well.
The second piece is how do we put together the right teams that come from applied AI backgrounds, but then also complement them with folks of industry and m and a.

kp.k: Physical work and churn constrain rollup suitability
kp.d: The screening framework excludes sectors where physical-world activity prevents at least 30% task automation and sectors with high customer churn, because implementation may involve six months to a year of disruption. A third constraint is present model quality: the strategy does not target tasks where AI currently performs worse than humans.
qs: It's not in, for example, you know, maybe plumbing and roofing and HVAC and a lot of like in person work, firefighting, etcetera.
So 1 bucket is that a second bucket is we don't want to go and buy up firms that are have high churn.

And so we also another big criteria is we're only doing this in industries where there are really good business dynamics, where the customers have sticky contracts, maybe they're multi year, there's very low churn.

So when we come in and we start doing AI automation, it's not always a 100% smooth. And so we have to have the benefit of at least 6 months or a year to kind of implement these things, for our base workers and for the end clients as well.
So there are also other industries where, oh, maybe 1 day AI could do those tasks, but the current models are worse than humans doing it. So you're not adding any real value there.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Marc Bhargava argues that AI-enabled service rollups can combine software, service delivery and acquisitions to expand capacity and margins, including by enabling corporate legal departments to outsource less.
pts.d: Bhargava describes acquiring service businesses as a way to obtain distribution, client relationships, proprietary data and faster feedback loops. He presents the legal portfolio company rendered variously as UDIA, Udia and Yudia in the transcript as selling Fortune 100 general counsel a combination of software and services, including NDA and contract tools; he reports its acquisition of a service business rendered as Johnson Hannah. The intended result is more work performed in-house with the same team and less expenditure on outside law firms. Across selected service industries, he claims that automating 30–70% of tasks can free workers for more demanding work rather than eliminate their occupations. He projects that, in certain cases, automation above 50% could support EBITDA margins of 30–40%, compared with 5–10%. His pricing thesis is more output at approximately the same price, rather than primarily cost cutting. He also predicts a qualitative change in legal services: comparing contracts and recommending pricing changes could make legal departments more proactive contributors to business performance. His preferred operating model combines automated steps with human work rather than complete autonomous service delivery.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Bhargava relies on General Catalyst's internal industry screening, workflow mapping, pilot-client data and portfolio-company experience; the financial and employment projections remain investment theses.
pts.d: At 9:27, Bhargava reports 50–70% automation of call-center workflows through Crescendo, 38% automation in an MSP/IT investment and 80% automation in bookkeeping through Kick. These are cross-domain portfolio reports, not legal-work automation measurements. At 28:42, he says screening 70 industries identified 10 with at least 30% automation potential. At 41:24–44:21, he describes shadowing workers, mapping workflows and hours, and requiring granular pilot evidence before providing acquisition capital. The transcript moves between percentages of tasks, workflows and hours without supplying a common measurement protocol. His legal examples concern an existing portfolio offering and his experience of model capabilities: he says OpenAI is strong at summarizing case text and Anthropic at reasoning and anticipating courtroom questions. He supplies no named legal benchmark, legal accuracy figures, independently verified margin results or quantified outside-counsel spending reductions. His broader job-creation forecast relies on historical technology analogies, labor-shortage arguments and portfolio experience; he expressly acknowledges uncertainty about net employment effects. These are Bhargava's accounts as an investor involved in the strategy, not independently established findings in the document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The strategy targets automation achievable with current tools, requires implementation time and customer growth, and uses a three-year revenue-doubling objective rather than a forecast of immediate full replacement.
pts.d: In this episode published August 2, 2025, Bhargava describes roughly two and a half years of strategy experience and improvements as models are released every three to six months. He excludes businesses he expects to become fully automated from this particular rollup strategy, and favors industries where human relationships, regulation, complexity and judgment support continued human participation. Acquisition candidates must demonstrate automation potential and a strong desire for technological change. Existing workflows are generally preserved to ease adoption. Low churn and sticky contracts are important because implementation may require six months to a year and may encounter difficulties; heavily physical work and tasks current models perform worse than humans are other exclusions. Revenue growth requires workers to gain actual capacity and the business to win additional clients. His broad underwriting objective is to double revenue over three years while increasing costs by 20% for software, engineering and AI tools; it is an investment target, not a reported realized outcome. The longer-run thesis also assumes continued access to competitive foundation models. He gives a subjective probability below 3% to a scenario in which all relevant providers close off access, citing the number of competing providers and open-source alternatives.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed beneficiaries are corporate legal buyers, service clients, retained service workers and owners who participate in rollups; outside law firms may lose outsourced work.
pts.d: For legal services, Bhargava specifically identifies Fortune 100 general counsel and in-house legal teams as buyers who can handle more work internally, with outside law firms receiving less outsourced work. This is an enterprise spending and capacity claim, not a claim about closing the civil justice gap. Lawyers, accountants, IT specialists, call-center staff and property or HOA managers are envisaged as retaining roles while automating mundane tasks and undertaking harder or more relationship-intensive work, sometimes managing teams of agents. Customers are promised more output at similar prices and potentially more proactive recommendations. Owners of acquired businesses are offered continued involvement and equity rollover, with participation in longer-term growth rather than a short private-equity holding period. Bhargava predicts that a majority of service firms could participate if they wish, because tools fit existing workflows and younger entrants are familiar with AI. He expects overall economic expansion and new jobs, while acknowledging that some types of jobs can decline and that the precise balance of losses and gains is difficult to predict.
